She said: Mr. Speaker, I rise today to speak to the motion which you have just put before this House:
That this House call upon the government as a matter of priority to ensure that the CBC be strengthened as an instrument of national identity providing local, regional, and national services to all Canadians.
This debate today is as much about Canada as it is about the CBC. I would suggest to you that it is a debate of serious national proportions, given the particular atmosphere that prevails across this land and the sensitivity that is being show or the lack of sensitivity that is being expressed in parts of our country.
The Prime Minister has called for national unity. I am quite delighted to see that he has even used the term national unity, since he wanted it expunged from the language of the Broadcasting Act. What could have been a more sensitive tool than the question of national unity through the Canadian broadcasting system, and particularly the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation.
He called as well for dialogue among Canadians, but a right now a lot of that dialogue has been one-shot deals, such as through the Spicer commission.
I would suggest that the most effective communication and communication vehicle we have in place across this land, infrastructure put in place and paid for by Canadians, is that of Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, better known as Radio-Canada CBC. It has its place and station identification from coast to coast to coast in English and in French: in the north, in the east, in the west, in the small urban communities, in the small rural communities across this land, in radio and TV as well as internationally. It certainly is a key medium of expression for all Canadians.
I would say that this debate today is about the kind of country we want and the kind of national institutions we

March 25, 1991
Supply
on this side of the House believe are fundamental. They are the fundamental infrastructure that binds and links Canadians. It is the highway of today that we were so proud of many years back, whether it is the Trans-Canada Highway or the laying of the last spike in the railway. I just hope we have not split the heart of this nation by laying the last spike of destruction into our Canadian national broadcasting system.
We see and hear all around us about the need to build bridges in this country and the fact that it is a pressing need. How better to communicate with each other than through radio and television?
Mr. Speaker, you are a communicator. You were in the media. You are a man who knows the power of words, the power of expression, the fact that you can reach the minds and hearts of our countrymen, country women, children and folks across this land. We can be folksy. We can be esoteric. We can be pragmatic. We can go to the heart of the matter and do it through news and information, but what better way than through entertainment, than with a smile, through poking a little fun at each other.
All the different cultures that surround us and enrich us become the tapestry which is the basis of our society, whether black, brown, yellow or white. Whatever the language, that language, that culture, that way of life, becomes part of what is the distinctive Canada we have been trying to build. We have been trying to say that we are tolerant. We have been trying to say that we are a wonderful country. And what do we do? The medium that best expresses who we are and what we are, we cut its throat.
When Mr. Veilleux, the president of CBC, said the other day that we are killing this communication vehicle through the back door, strangling it through budget cuts, he was saying it as it is and calling the shot.
I appeared before the CRTC with 12 of my colleagues. We made three hours of presentation before the CRTC indicating that we could ill afford not to pay for this particular service, that we could ill afford to cut this service. If the president, the chairman of the board and the board of the CBC really were concerned for this country, were really carrying out the mandate of the National Broadcasting Act, which we just finished revising, they would have looked at it. They would have tried to make changes. They would have cut where there was duplication. They would have cut more and perhaps
revised more. In the end they would have realized that we could not realize a proper French and English, multiracial, multicultural broadcasting corporation serving the three coasts of Canada. They would have resigned if they had had any kind of good conscience. This minister, they knew, never went and pleaded the cause for Radio-Canada CBC before the Treasury Board. I do not know what he said to his cabinet colleagues but, if he told them the truth, then the whole cabinet should resign.
What is happening with Radio-Canada and Radio Canada International, which I know is one of your interests, Mr. Speaker, is an utter disgrace. It is an absolute disgraces that the parliamentary channel might be privatized. It belongs to the people of this land.
I do not understand the priorities of this government. I do not understand. Even though we are in a budgetary crisis, even though we have financial concerns, and all of us share those concerns, there is still a matter of choice and a matter of priority. That priority right now is keeping this country going. That priority right now is affecting the kind of place and space for all Canadians regardless of their mother tongue, regardless of their colour, regardless of their race, regardless of their creed.
The new bill which this government has not even bothered to gazette brings in some very important new features. It bring in the whole question of the Official Languages Act. The 1968 bill took place before the Official Languages Act became part of this country. It came into force in 1969. It took place before employment equity and all the safeguards around section 15, the non-discriminatoiy clause, came into effect in 1982 in the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
We have ignored the Charter of Rights and Freedoms. We have ignored the Official Languages Act. We have ignored the new Broadcasting Act which says use independent producers, make sure that we use our creative talents through artistic expression, through entertainment, and what do we have? We have a mock CNN and a mock Newsworld, and a great big Media Watch or I should say meteorological station which is going to tell us the big weather news and give us the big sports news.
However, what is happening in small towns? What is happening in the regions? Canada is more than just a province. That is the way the CBC has seen it, just as a province. We have 10 provinces and a distinct territory, but we do not happen to have some distinctions, let us say, in Ontario.
March 25, 1991

Let me take Quebec first. We have no distinctions in Quebec?
[ Translation]
-the Eastern Townships, the Outaouais, the Gaspe and the North Shore all have very specific identities. And you can't reflect those from Montreal and Quebec City alone. That won't work. The people of Rimouski, Ma-tane and Sept-Iles where you cut regional programming and left a tremendous void are not pleased with what your colleagues on the other side of this House have done. It is totally unacceptable.

If we move into Ontario, are they trying to tell me that the northern part of Ontario looks like Toronto or looks like the Ottawa region? When we are driving along the 417 from Montreal to Ottawa or from any other part of this province such as the 401 to Toronto, or from the other provinces, we should find out about the weather and the traffic control. With this government's options and the way things are going, there are going to be more people on the 401. The point is that we cannot possibly entertain the suggestion that the province of Ontario has two spots that will reflect its entire personality: Ottawa and Toronto.
I suppose Windsor does not count. It got lost among our five large lakes of which we should be very proud. We forgot them. We just left them to languish with no voice either public or private in the Windsor area.
Then we go out to the prairies, and on the French side what do we have?

Don't we have a responsibility to reflect the specific culture of Francophones outside Quebec, their view of society, for their own benefit and the benefit of all Canadians? Hardly. We are cutting right and left. We cut Genies en herbe; Ce soir dimanche; Actualites regionales; Le lien. Cuts are being made all over Canada. In Vancouver, and Regina, in the official language, the language of minorities outside Quebec. Do you think that is fair? Do you think that makes sense? Do you think it's a good idea? Do you want to pursue this policy and expect to have a Canada for everyone, a united Canada from coast
Supply
to coast? This is madness, Mr. Speaker, and it is intolerable!
I started out to say that this is what this country is all about, why Canada needs to be protected from this government that brought in a recession. On the back of that recession, it is now saying that it has to cut one of the major infrastructures that link this country; Radio-Canada, the CBC. I am saying that this is not the way we are to go about structuring our country.
The issues basically are: Do the airwaves belong to the public? Do they belong to us and are we holding that trust for the public here in this House, whether it is the public or the private sector, or do they belong to the board of directors? Do we expect the private sector to do the job of the public sector, because after all, they are a business? The public sector, in this instance is a business, but it is more than a business. It is not the ordinary business of the country, it is the special business of the country. It involves the talent of this country.
We live next to a wonderful neighbour, a giant, my American cousins. They are experts in the technique of communication. They have found the way to globalize entertainment, to show a portrait of a society that is not ours, but is amusing and entertaining. But, is that all there is to life, American entertainment, American sitcoms and an American way of seeing the world? Is there not a Canadian vision we wish to promote out there? If there is a Canadian vision how, in a communicating society, because that is what we are in, can we show it if we do not support both the Canadian Council and Radio-Canada?
We cannot allow the board of directors to take over the issue of the airwaves. It belongs to the public. Does the CRTC regulate public broadcasting in Canada or does that responsibility lie with the CBC as a self-regulating board? That is a very serious question and it needs to be addressed in a very serious manner. Are the laws of Canada, namely the Broadcasting Act, either the 1968 act or, if this government ever gets around to gazetting the 1990 act, to be respected as they reflect the wishes of Parliament, or can they be changed, as I said, through the backdoor, through government allocations?

March 25, 1991

Fourth, are the local, regional and national broadcasters and broadcasting to be interpreted as provincial? What happened to local and regional that is in the bill? Since when are the regions provinces? That is the way the board has seen them.
Fifth, the mandate of the new act includes, and I think I outlined the fact, the parliamentary will as expressed through the Official Languages Act and through the Charter of Rights and Freedoms.
I would suggest that the revisions presented by the board of directors, its president and its chairman, must be reviewed by Parliament. It is a matter of priority and the CBC should so direct following its hearings. It is a very disquieting moment in the history of our country.
I noted a very interesting comment which the President of the CBC, Mr. Veilleux made. The day he appeared before the CRTC, he was outlining his vision of a restructured CBC. In particular, he talked about his vision, which he translated into a programming agenda. He outlined five key elements. The first one is enough to make one stop: "A CBC that offers strong national services which are rooted in the regions of the country." The question is, if one looks at the programming what did he mean by the word "regions" and what can we possibly think he meant by the word "local"? Did he know that it was in the bill? Did the members of that board know it was in the bill?
He then goes on to mention the whole question of a mirror. I thought it was a very interesting quote he used, which I would like to bring to your attention. He says:
What the CBC is trying to do in English and French television is
replace a mirror with a window.
Instead of replacing the mirror with a window, he should have said he was replacing it with a slammed-shut window because I would like to know how the window is going to be open in so many places across this land. You tell me how the window is open in Windsor; you tell me how it in open in Matane; you tell me how it is open in Sept lies; you tell me how it is open in Windsor. Mr. Veilleux should go back to his board and tell them to reopen the window he thought was opening-because he didn't open it. It needs to be smashed open, if that is his vision.
I would like to know how Calgary TV viewers are going to be served by Edmonton. I would like to know whether it is better to have a one-hour show that is going to include Edmonton and Calgary, instead of the two hours they presently have.
I would like to suggest that Mr. Veilleux go back to the drawing board, and so does the CBC.
First of all, I was in Newfoundland where we just left them floating out in the sea. We have cut so much in Newfoundland and Labrador, but I am sure my colleagues will talk about that. But let us look at Moncton. Programs like Tele-Debate, Tele-Debat, La Revue, Spec Art have already been cut. As I said, Genies en herbe and Musicologie-l mean, we don't have to know anything about music. After all, if we listen to the news we will know everything, we will be so well informed-we will be ignoramuses in this world.
I would say that they are not going to review Les Jeux d'Acadie. Is it not important that people in Prince Edward Island and the rest of Canada can have a sense of profound joy as they look at our youth who are involved in sports, who are showing competence and the potential to become international figures in the world of sport? But, no, we cut that out because it is not important.
Mr. Speaker, all regional programs have been cut except news. Well, I don't know if you agree with me, but I think Canadians are more than news junkies; I think Canadians are interested in a variety of entertainment, so that they can see themselves and find out who they are.
As I move along I would like to point out to you that our party believes that Canada is more than its regions, that Canada is rooted in the realities of its small communities, their singers and performers, their values, their stories. It is the fact that Newfoundland is more than an outport and the west is more than a wheat field. It is more than just the local focus, but the local focus feeds into the regional, which becomes part of the national, and it is how you build a star system. It is how you get to know the Simards of this world, how you get to know the Ann Murrays of this world. It is a way in which you can feel that you belong.

I think A1 Johnson said it best when he said; "The public broadcasting service, to have to reconcile itself to being a network service, would be a little like saying let us have a Canada without the provinces".
I would suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that that speaks reams for the vision of my colleagues across the floor.
One of the things that we can ill-afford to do is not promote this vision of Canada. In a time of great financial restraint such as now, in a time when, yes, we must be addressing the deficit, we also have to remember there is a future. If we want to have a sense of belonging, a sense of participation, a sense of peoplehood, a sense of nation, and be prepared to pay for our public broadcaster, then we have to have it rooted in the local community. We have to have a sense of belonging so that our hearts and our minds, of our children and of our public, will be prepared to pay and to continue paying for this excellent service that is the envy of the world, Mr. Speaker.
I only have a minute left. There were a few people I had wanted to bring to your attention. I am afraid that time is of the essence, but I want to point out that-

-Canada's diversity, its magnificent geography, its many languages and cultures, and current political events that are so important to us, are so many reasons why we need a strong Pan-Canadian voice. Therefore, we believe that the CBC must continue to play its public interest role, in other words, to help communicate to Canadians a national spirit, a national awareness that will give them a sense of pride and develop a sense of national unity.
I would say to you that in a real sense, television is to 20th century Canada what the railway was to the 19th. Its visual productions are the medium that allows thousands of Canadians to hear and see themselves.
If I may, I would like to close with a quote from the former Ambassador of Canada to the United States, Mr. Allan Gotlieb, because I believe as he was negotiating the free trade agreement he recognized culture. He said this, and with this I will close: "The communications revolution and the emergence of the homogenizing

The principal challenge for the state today in the cultural sphere is to foster the creation of the content that is carried on those electronic systems and on video screens. The spectacular growth of the homogenized universal software has made this one of the primary national tasks of our time".

Mr. Speaker, I listened very carefully to what was said by the hon. member for Mount Royal. We are very much aware of her competence in this area. I read in her motion, and I quote:
- providing local, regional and national services to all Canadians.
She has been working on this matter for several months, and she has had an interest in communications for many years. I would like to ask her the following question, and I would appreciate a sincere answer: Did you get or did you have access to all the details on CBC expenditures, including the salaries of all journalists, members of the board of directors, employees, overtime, and especially spending on coverage of national events, and spending per station? When we talk about $1.4 billion annually, this means that the corporation is entirely free to spend $1.4 billion without being accountable to Parliament. And even that is easy. Every year I receive a nice annual report with a glossy cover and a couple of thousand dollars-just a financial report. But in municipalities, like my own town of Val-d'Or or Matane, Gaspe or Sept-iles, every month residents can check expenditures by their elected representatives and the municipality.
My question is this: Did the hon. member, since she has contacts at the CBC, obtain all the details, not just what it says in the Estimates but details that are confidential, including all expenditures and salaries? Did you have access to that list?

I thank my hon. colleague from Toronto for that question. It is one of the prime questions and it is one of the issues at stake here.
Can the CBC continue to collect advertising revenue when it is not present in the community, when it cannot help the local businessman so that he can prosper along the way? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for Mount Royal for her motion today seeking that the CBC be strengthened as an instrument of national identity. However, I regret that she seems unaware of the fact that this strengthening process has already begun. It is under way through efforts of this government in introducing and the passage of Bill C-40, which the hon. member assisted in committee and which will be proclaimed shortly.
In fact, there is no need for this motion.
Indeed, the hon. member's energies would best assist the broadcasting system if she were to recognize that this government is working to preserve Canada's entire broadcasting system, both the public and private, and that only through renewed sensitivity to public environments and needs will broadcasters be able to assure all Canadians of their own unique structure for communications.
Perhaps some background would be helpful for members.
Let me remind the hon. member of the government's support of the CBC mandate. In a speech of the Minister of Communications of January 31, 1990 when he addressed the Legislative Committee on Bill C-40, he said:
I have frequently said that this Crown corporation must be the cornerstone for expression of our cultural reality. It is in this spirit that we tabled before the Parliament of Canada this broadcasting bill, which, for the first time, gives the CBC a mandate to contribute more actively to cultural expression and to the exchange of the various forms it can take. The CBC must distinguish itself from private broadcasters. This is also the first time we have taken a legislative route to ask the CBC to reflect not on our unity alone, but on our cultural identity.
The minister addresses this issue directly, from the beginning. Nor has the position of this government changed. The broadcasting bill which this House has deliberated on and passed specifies a mandate to rejuvenate the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and which clarifies its responsibilities with respect to Canadian, regional and cultural programming needs.
For the first time, this mandate includes specific references to the important role that the CBC has in reflecting Canada, in providing English and French programming services, in meeting the needs of official language minorities, in reflecting Canadian society in all its aspects, in actively contributing to the flow and exchange of cultural expression and, in these ways, contributing to a shared Canadian consciousness and identity.
Certain critics have lamented the removal of the phrase "national unity" from the CBC's mandate, yet there can be no doubt that the objectives which are cited here will indeed contribute to Canadian unity.
The Minister of Communications, speaking before this House on the occasion of the third reading of Bill C-40 on December 4, 1990, asks:
How can there be unity without the flow and exchange of cultural expression in English, and in French, among all component parts in Canada, as foreseen by this bill. And how can there be unity without a shared awareness of Canadian identity?
Let me turn now to the generous support given the CBC by this government. Yes, much is expected of this corporation; however, despite cries to the contrary from certain quarters, it should be recognized that a great deal has also been given and is being given to the CBC to meet these objectives.

Let us look at CBC Radio. From the very beginning of public broadcasting when it was the only technology available, radio has been a keystone of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Our public stereo and monaural broadcast channels have become the envy of much of the world, and rightly so. It can be said without contradiction that the programming developed for English and French language radio services are uniquely Canadian in tone and have provided an important link in our cultural infrastructure.
The CBC has recently enhanced the quality of these services in many communities by making them available on new FM frequencies. For their part the stereo networks provide Canadian listeners with an alternative music selection, as well as foreground programming and theatre.
Partly because radio is a less expensive medium than television, it has been virtually unaffected by the measures announced by the CBC board. That CBC Radio is vulnerable to economic circumstances, as reflected in future budgets; is a fact; however, the goodwill of Parliament toward continued support of these valuable services can be in no doubt.
The hon. member mentioned in her address the Northern Services. We would be remiss if we were not to recognize at this time the importance of the CBC Northern Services. They bring radio and television programming to the Yukon and the Northwest Territories and to the northern regions of Quebec in seven native languages as well as in English and French. This service and other regional programming already scheduled or in planning will ensure that all Canadians are in communication with mainstream thought as well as in having the opportunity to meet each other.
In closing, this government recognizes the role played by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation within the larger framework of the Canadian broadcasting system. We have clearly supported this public broadcaster and have every intention to continue to do so. As the same time we require it to act within its mandate as defined by Parliament and to plan responsibly within the resources that this Parliament provides after much thought and deliberation.
We do not come to such decisions lightly or capriciously. In appointing persons of the high quality whom we now see serving on the board of directors of the
Supply
Canadian Broadcasting Corporation, we place confidence in their administrative decisions and are firm in our belief that they will be innovative and faithful stewards of this public trust.

Mr. Speaker, James Bay II is the largest hydroelectric project ever conceived in the history of North America, and the clear-cutting for the flooding has begun without environmental impact evaluation.
Twenty years ago the James Bay Development Corporation of Quebec launched its scheme to restrain or divert all the major rivers of James Bay and northern Quebec, creating a gigantic series of dams, dikes, and reservoirs.
Premier Bourassa then as now made it clear that the purpose was to provide power to the United States. Cost estimates for James Bay I rose from $1 billion when it began to over $24 billion for its completion in 1996.
The real costs to the Cree, to the Inuit, and to Canada's environment are devastating. Once the land is flooded it is lost forever. Mercury laden fish, drowned caribou, ruined habitat for the Beluga whales and for hundreds of other species, and flooding from the two phases of 26,000 square kilometres, 2 per cent of the entire province of Quebec, six times as much land flooded by this project as is protected in all of its provincial and national parks combined.
The federal and provincial governments are playing a treacherous game in allowing this project to proceed in bits and pieces without an over-all environmental assessment. Even worse, the alternatives to this project are being purposely hidden from Canadians and Quebecers.

TRIBUTE TO THE LATE HON. LEON BALCER
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise in the House today to join all my colleagues in the House of Commons in paying tribute to the Hon. Leon Balcer who died this weekend at the age of 73. Mr. Balcer was a member of this House and a cabinet minister for many years. He was first elected member of Parliament for Trois-Rivieres in 1949. He served his constituents in the electoral district of Trois-Rivieres for six consecutive terms, which at the time was a record for a member from Quebec elected to the House of Commons.
March 25, 1991

Mr. Balcer also served as a minister under the late John Diefenbaker, from 1957 to 1965. He held the post of Solicitor General of Canada, was a member of the Treasury Board and, towards the end of his career, was Minister of Transport. Mr. Balcer finished his political career as an independent member in the House and subsequently tried to start a career in provincial politics which unfortunately proved unsuccessful.
Mr. Balcer also served as a naval officer during World War II on the Annan, one of the ships that helped hunt down German submarines, and he felt he learned a great deal from this experience.
The former member for Trois-Rivieres and minister and member of the Privy Council was a man of great dedication, so much so that he had earned the respect of all his constituents, whatever their political stripe.
This weekend, in the Trois-Rivieres newspaper Le Nouvelliste, journalist Jacques Laberge wrote that Mr. Balcer would be remembered as a member of Parliament who served the interests of his riding with loyalty and dedication. I am sure that all members of this House will join me today in offering our sincere condolences to all the people who knew Mr. Balcer and especially the members of his family.

He had a sense of his country, a sense of history, a deep-seated sense of what Canada was and of his place as French-speaking Leon Balcer both in the Progressive Conservative Party of Canada and in this House, and we are grateful to him for greats memories. He accom-

plished a lot more than a number of members can ever expect to do in their lifetime. He was a member of this House in very trying times. He had earned the respect of all his colleagues and of the Right Hon. Louis St. Laurent.

Still, in these few words, on behalf of my party and of my colleague Mr. Gray who also knew him well and who is the senior member of the House of Commons, I want to offer our most sincere condolences to his family.

Mr. Speaker, it is a sad comment that one of the rare occasions that brings unanimity to this House is when we pay tribute to those who have passed on. On behalf of the government and, I am sure, on behalf of all members of this House, I would like to pay tribute to Pauline Vanier, the wife of one of Canada's governor generals, of a general with a brilliant career and of a Canadian ambassador.
I had the pleasure of meeting him more than 40 years ago on my first trip to France when I, a young Quebecer, marched up to the embassy and asked to meet the ambassador, and so, I had that privilege. I was very impressed. General Vanier's military career had instilled in him a certain rigour which some called rigidity-and great strength of character and discipline which, in turn, he expected of those around him. I think his wife provided an additional dimension because she was, which was unusual even then, not only a remarkable wife but also a remarkable woman as such, with many admirable qualities and also very efficient. In each of the difficult roles her husband was asked to play, she was at his side, and I think she made Canadians take pride in their representative, especially as their head of State.
She was an inspiration to her husband and to all Canadians who met her, and she presided over the destinies of this country at a time when it was making its mark in history. On behalf of the government I wish to express our sincere condolences to all her children and other members of her family.

Mr. Speaker, a great lady has passed away. With the death of Pauline Vanier, last Saturday, we certainly lost the last member of a real princely couple. We all know the work done by Mr. Georges P. Vanier as Governor General. We also know the work he accomplished with the 22nd Regiment which was known as Vandoo across the country. But we know also that in the Vanier family, Mrs. Vanier gave women an opportunity for fulfilment.
The Canadian Encyclopedia describes the work that Mrs. Vanier accomplished for our poor, our youth and our families. It was not only the work of her husband, but hers, as a person. She was chancelor at the University of Ottawa. She was also a powerful force in the establishment of the Vanier Institute of the Family and everybody across Canada knows that it was Mrs. Vanier who encouraged her son to create the Arche community, which gives hope to those who lost it.
With a family as highly regarded as the Vanier family, we realize that it was the mother, the wife and the woman who was able in all circumstances to give the support that was needed, but it is also true that now-
With the death of Pauline Vanier, we have lost part of a great Canadian family. We have also lost a women who, through her own inspiration, has left a monument to her family that will outlive any of her children, or grandchildren, or great-grandchildren.
Of course her work as Chancellor of the University of Ottawa was extremely well known. Less well known was the influence that she played in the life of her son and the establishment of l'Arche homes for those who really need the help.
Most particular, where I personally have a great respect for the Vanier family was in the work that she did in establishing the Vanier Institute for the Family. The family is a changing institution and even today as we speak the Vanier Institute is able to be on the cutting edge of social reform. At a time when the country is

March 25, 1991

Speaker's Ruling PRIVILEGE
crying out for support of the new family, not just the traditional family, Madam Vanier has made the study of new families, the study of social policy, and in particular the assistance for those who really need it one of her life goals.
Of course she will be missed by her children and her grandchildren, but she will also be missed by all of those who feel that it is the responsibility of someone in public life to help, to support, and to provide inspiration to those who cannot help themselves. Indeed that has been the hallmark of the life of the Vanier family, and the person behind that great hallmark was indeed Madam Vanier.

I must now advise the House with respect to a question of privilege which was raised on Thursday, March 21, by the House leader of the Official Opposition, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, concerning the government advertisements which appeared in newspapers on March 16, 1991 relating to budget highlights.
The advertisement in question entitled "Canada's Plan for Economic Recovery" describes an eight-page newsletter which will be sent to every household explaining important highlights of the 1991 budget recently presented by the Minister of Finance.
The newsletter itself described economic initiatives taken by the government regarding inflation, the national debt, and interest rates. It also describes the government's plan to control expenditures to reduce the deficit, noting among other matters that legislation will be introduced to establish the debt servicing reduction fund.
I might say that on a number of occasions in the document the suggestion is made that legislation will be introduced.
In his presentation, the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond argued that by placing the advertisements in newspapers across the country the Minister of Finance acted as if the House had already passed the budget. He went on to suggest that the ad misrepresented the budget document tabled in the House and made several references to the ruling of October 10, 1989 concerning the advertisement on the goods and services tax.

In support of these arguments, the house leader for the New Democratic Party, the hon. member for Kamloops, rose to claim that not only were the advertisements contemptuous and misleading, but they also prejudiced the decision of the House on the budget.

In reply, the hon. Minister of Finance stated that he had followed the directions of the Chair as laid down in the ruling of October 10, 1989. He argued that the advertising had made it clear that these were budget

March 25, 1991
Point of Order
proposals and quoted from the brief note in the newsletter he himself signed: "This budget proposes far-reaching initiatives." He then went on to argue that, contrary to the contention of the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond, the advertisements accurately represented the 1991 budget document tabled in the House.
The interventions on March 21 touch on three major issues: whether the newsletter misrepresents the budget document; whether, in sponsoring this advertising the Minister of Finance acted as if the House had already passed the budget; and whether the advertisement will prejudice a future decision of the House.
On the first question, that is, whether the newsletter misrepresents the budget document, the Chair really has no role to play since it is clearly a dispute as to fact. The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond and the hon. Minister of Finance have different views on the government's economic initiatives and on the manner in which the newsletter presents those initiatives. The Chair can only conclude that the disagreement between the two hon. members is a matter of debate which could more properly be addressed in another forum. It is, with respect, not a question of privilege.
Another issue raised concerned the actions of the minister in authorizing these advertisements, and whether or not he was acting as if the House had already passed the budget motion.
To the information of all hon. members and the viewing public, on February 26 at the beginning of his budget speech, the Minister of Finance moved a motion reading: "That this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the government." Following this, the rules of the House establish that there is a six-day debate ending with the decision on whether or not the government's budgetary policy has the support of the House. In the present case, a decision has not yet been taken. There are two days remaining in the budget debate.
The hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond contends that the minister should have waited until a decision of the House was taken on this motion before the advertisements were made. The minister replied that the newsletter was intended to satisfy the needs of Canadians to understand what was being proposed in the complex budget documents. The newsletter was careful to explain that these were proposals and that legislation would soon be introduced.
The Chair has to conclude that prima facie there is no breach of privilege or contempt of the House in this regard since the minister was careful in respecting the role of the House in these matters and indicated in the newsletter that these were proposals.

Another issue raised by the hon. member for Kamloops was that these advertisements prejudiced the decision that the House is to take. I would refer all hon. members to the ruling of October 10, 1989, at page 4460 of Hansard:
"The House and its committees do not work in a vacuum. Members are constantly aware of outside factors and pressures. Since no threats or bribes have been made, it is difficult to see how the work of the House has been prejudiced or which specific privilege has been breached."

I cannot see how these advertisements can prejudice the decision which the House will take on the budget motion. The purpose of the newsletter was to disseminate information and the Chair is satisfied that it did so in full respect of the authority of this House.
I want to thank the hon. Minister of Finance, and the hon. member for Kamloops for their contributions on the matter raised, as I said earlier, succinctly by the hon. member for Cape Breton-East Richmond. After carefully reviewing the material itself and having considered all the arguments presented, I must conclude, however, prima facie, there is no breach of privilege.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to participate in the debate this afternoon. The motion that my colleague from Mount Royal has put before the House is a very appropriate motion. As we know, it deals with the current situation which the CBC faces with the severe financial cutbacks and is a question that must address the future of this corporation in Canada and the future role that it plays in building a unique Canadian identity.
The CBC is an institution with a troubled future. Over the last decade, chronic reductions in the level of funding have left the CBC virtually impoverished and unable to provide for Canadians the truly national presence that is its mandate. The mandate stretches back to the creation of the CBC in 1932 as the Canadian Radio Broadcasting Commission. A crucial element of

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
this mandate was the recognition of the need to foster a sense of national community and to be able to act as an instrument or a tool which allows Canadians a sense of self. Yet today, Canada remains a nation that is virtually awash in foreign culture.
That is why the preservation of the uniqueness of our Canadian way of life has meant that special consideration has to be given to our cultural industries and to our tools of communication, such as public broadcasting through the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Unfortunately over the last seven years, the actions of the federal government which have been committed to implementing a U.S. style market-driven economy, have seriously reduced the CBC's allocation of resources and hence its ability to adequately fulfil its public mandate. If we go back and look at the budgetary allocations to the CBC, since 1984, when inflation is taken into consideration, we find that expenditures in real dollar allocations to the CBC have been reduced by hundreds of millions of dollars.
There is also in place now a plan to cut back another $140 million from the CBC's operation expenditures over the next four years.
Few organizations can be expected to operate properly when they have this kind of a financial broad axe hanging over its head. That is exactly what this government is expecting of the CBC; to make do with less by either cutting services, which it has already had to do, or to make up the losses by relying more and more on a commercial revenue base, as the CBC has also had to do. This kind of chronic underfunding by the federal government has forced the CBC to rely increasingly on commercial revenues.
In looking at the current situation, approximately 30 per cent of the CBC's revenues are gained through increased reliance on the marketplace. That has seriously compromised the corporation's ability to develop the kind of unique Canadian programming and the unique Canadian broadcasting that is required to have this corporation act as a tool of national unity and an instrument of national identity.
Such reliance on commercial revenues has already, and I submit will continue, to blur the distinction between public broadcasting on the one hand and private broadcasting on the other. Hence, it will continue to blur
the distinction of the essence of the CBC. This is not a criticism of CBC management. It is just a reality of the marketplace. It is what is going to happen when you have to rely more and more on commercial revenues. You will have to mimic our U.S. partners, American programming, which has a greater revenue base, attracts more advertising revenue. When you start to mimic that you lose your sense of identity, as the CBC is already beginning to do.
Faced with these fiscal restraints, few options are available to the CBC. Through this gradual submersion into the commercial marketplace, the quintessential Canadian identity of the CBC is being lost. It is being subverted and it is losing its mandate, as I said, to act as an essential tool of nation building.
Soon, if things continue the way they have, all that will remain for this government will be to sell off the pieces to the highest bidder.
Back in 1929 the Aird royal commission on broadcasting at that time concluded that if broadcasting was going to be commercial then it was going to be American. If broadcasting was going to be Canadian, then it was going to have to be public. Back then, Graham Spry, the founder of the Canadian Radio League probably phrased it best when he said, in referring to Canadian broadcasting: "It will either be the state or the United States". I submit that the latter may very well be the consequence for the CBC if we continue with this chronic erosion of public funding.
To their credit, the management of the CBC has tried to make the best out of what is essentially an intolerable situation. Despite the onerous cuts they have presented to the CRTC, the $108 million funding shortfall, and the fact that they have had to slash and basically throw 1,100 workers on to the street, the CBC has simply tried to rationalize as best it can how to operate with this significant reduction in funding levels.
I mentioned the sacrifice of 1,100 jobs, the severing of over 140 local programs, many of which are distinguished examples of what is best about the CBC. Although I disagree with their actions, I understand exactly why they have had to do it. It has been an act that has been brought about, I submit, by a government that is essentially committed to the demise of public broadcasting in Canada.
March 25, 1991

Mr. Veilleux's choices were brutal as president of the CBC. But what options did he have? In an effort to keep the CBC alive his actions, although necessary, have only served to emasculate the CBC and to facilitate this government's agenda.
The government has tried to hide from it, has tried to hide behind the argument that it has nothing to do with the CBC cuts. That was a board decision. That was a decision of the management of the CBC. The fact remains that those decisions would never have been made if the government had not left the corporation twisting in the wind to the tune of $108 million.
I talked with Mr. Veilleux. I talked with Mr. Watson. I asked them: "How many times did you try to see the Minister of Communications and meet with him to discuss this problem?" Their answer was that the Minister of Communications was invisible, that he would not meet with them, that he never offered them a minute of time in discussing the impact of throwing 1,100 people out in the street and reducing the operations in its 11 regional broadcast centres. The minister would not even take the time of day to meet with the management of the CBC. The government is simply trying to abdicate its responsibility in terms of allowing this corporation to do the job that it is through legislation mandated to do.
The CBC's choices, necessary, unfortunate, tragic, simply reflect the economic dynamics of the day. As Mr. Veilleux pointed out recently in the submission to the CRTC, Canadian society is changing and so must the CBC. The fact is that the choices that the CBC was forced to make reflect new values in our Canadian society. They reflect the neo-conservative market-driven values that have been the hallmark of this administration right from the free trade agreement through the GST and onward. I submit to you, Sir, that those market-driven, social Darwinian values are not reflective of the needs, or the wants or desires, of the Canadian people.
Under the Broadcasting Act which is still empowered, still in force until the royal proclamation of Bill C-40, the CBC may in fact be considered to be in violation of sections of that act. I refer to the revised statutes and this is what it says in referring to the CBC: "The National Broadcasting Service should be extended to all
Government Orders
parts of Canada, should be in French and English serving the special needs of the various geographic regions" and last, "should contribute to the development, national unity, and provide for a continuing expression of Canadian identity".
The action that the CBC board has had to take in light of the refusal of this government to fund it adequately is that it is no longer able to meet the requirements that are laid out in that legislation. At a time when Canada is a nation at a crossroads, a nation, I submit, with an uncertain future, for this government to unravel and to dismantle what is essentially a critical tool of nation building through our public broadcasting system is absolute heresy.
It makes no sense whatsoever. That is why the restructuring of the CBC services have to be closely examined and revisited. We are doing that now in the submissions that are being made even today at the CRTC hearings.
I would like to applaud the efforts of the CRTC in going ahead to hold those public hearings even though it is admitted that it really does not have any power to force the CBC to change its course of action.
As the federal regulatory agency, I think it does have the ability to send a very strong and unequivocal message to this government, a message that I think and hope will reflect the extent of the public concerned and the outrage that is being presented at the CRTC hearings as we speak in the House today.
The president of the CBC, Mr. Veilleux, was adamant that the management of the CBC would not be responsible for the next round of cuts, which already loom before us; the necessity of cutting yet another $50 million to $60 million and the necessity of cutting yet another 500 to 600 jobs.
He served notice that he and the chairman-designate, Patrick Watson, are no longer willing to serve as scapegoats for this administration.
Earlier in the week at the same hearings, Mr. Veilleux stated that with future funding cuts, the CBC would no longer be able to maintain its mandate. He warned, very clearly, that it would be up to Parliament to decide on the future of Canadian broadcasting. That sounds very much, to me, like a threat of resignation.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
Perhaps that is exactly what this government needs in order that it wake up and smell the coffee, in order that it begin to understand the serious nature of these funding reductions that it has visited upon the CBC.
Chairman-designate Patrick Watson just the other day was commenting on the public comments that the Prime Minister had made in relation to the CBC.
In an article here in The Toronto Star, Mr. Watson is saying that the Prime Minister is playing games with the people of Canada in a way that expresses a lofty kind of contempt for all those people who have lost jobs and all those communities that have had service taken away from them. There is even contempt for the process that is going on here in front of the CRTC.
I do not think it is worthy of a Prime Minister. I do not think the management of the CBC is willing to take any more in response to this government's mandate of dismantling and emasculating Canadian public broadcasting. I want to say to you, Mr. Speaker, that all areas of Canada are concerned about the effects of the cutbacks in the CBC.
I have a letter that arrived in my office today from the office of the Leader of the New Democratic Party in Nova Scotia. It is addressed to the CBC management, and signed by the Leader of the Nova Scotia New Democratic Party, Alexa McDonough. She says: "I am writing with regard to the proposal for a nightly English TV news magazine which was presented to the corporation at the opening of this week's CRTC hearings."
She goes on to talk about the concern of the loss of local broadcasting, and she says: "At the root of many policy disasters in this region is the failure of those in Ottawa, Toronto and Montreal to hear the men and women who catch and process our fish, who tend our wood lots and who work in our pulp mills, who grow our food and who care for our land. It is absurd to imagine that a nightly news magazine program produced in Toronto, regardless of how many maritime reporters it employed could satisfactorily replace Land and Sea", which, of course is one of the local programs that was axed in the round of cuts.
She goes on to warn that the people in this region properly expect that their public television network can and will serve our environment and the people who rely upon our vital resource industries.
That message is coming through loud and clear from Nova Scotia, the Atlantic provinces, Newfoundland, the Yukon, British Columbia, through our prairie provinces. Canadians are upset and angry with the cutbacks this government has visited upon the CBC.
I want to point out that this government is not the only one that should be blamed for the erosion of CBC funding, because it began some time ago. In fact, our Liberal colleagues made the initial round of cuts way back in 1978. They started the ball rolling by cutting back $78 million, which at that time amounted to 12 per cent of the CBC's budget for 1979-80.
I can go on, Mr. Speaker. We look at 1984 when this government first came to power, we see a reduction of $85 million. In 1985 a reduction of $45 million. In 1986 another $48 million. In 1989 we find, phasing over the next few years, a $140 million funding shortfall.
This leaves the CBC with essentially no choice in the matter. If it cannot make up the revenues through government-allocated expenditures, then it has to rely more on the commercial revenues that will shift its focus away from truly Canadian programming to the more Americanized type of programming. These shows, although granted they are popular-and I am sure all of us watch them from time to time-we have to also remember that these shows do not mirror the Canada which we are trying to present and develop in terms of its distinctive Canadian identify.
We have seen the closures of the three stations at Goose Bay, Matane and Toronto, and the reduction of eight other stations to operating essentially as news bureaus.
We have seen a $12 million cut to network TV and only this weekend -and we were discussing this earlier in the House today-the cutting of funds for Radio Canada International. I think it is an absolute disgrace that this government would allow an institution, Radio Canada International, which basically serves as Canada's voice to the world, being completely disassembled by the reduced funding at this level.
Mr. Speaker, I see you are indicating that my time is up. I had much more to add to the debates, but perhaps I will have an opportunity to do so during the questions that follow. I thank you for your time today.
March 25, 1991

wont for them to do, they will reach the point of no return in terms of their own ability to continue to serve.

They are not without blame, but I want to refocus the cross-hairs on the appropriate target, that is the Prime Minister this government that is hell-bent for election on the demise of public broadcasting in Canada.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION

Mr. Speaker, I appreciate the opportunity to ask my colleague a question with regard to the very excellent remarks that he made.
Many people are perhaps not aware that CBC coverage in fact had never been able to keep up with the mandate provided to it by Parliament.
For instance, in my constituency of Prince Albert- Churchill River, there are thousands of people who do not receive any kind of Saskatchewan television news coverage. There is no Saskatchewan station on cable systems or rebroadcast systems in many northern Saskatchewan communities. Those people certainly cannot follow the debate on public issues within that province nor see cultural or entertainments shows originating in that province, even though they are supposed to be a part of it. They already feel very isolated, and this just increases the feelings of isolation.
Second, with the closure of the Saskatoon station, it means that those northern communities in my constituency that did receive some CBC coverage through cable or whatever, are now reliant on a CBC signal out of Regina, and northern Saskatchewan news is never covered by that CBC station in Regina. It just does not have the resources to do it.
Virtually half the province is without CBC coverage. Is that the kind of thing we can expect more of? Are northern Canadians just the vanguard?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my colleague presents a very valid argument, the essence of which is very clear. When they move away from local broadcasting and centralize the operations with essentially one bureau in each of what they call the regions, which really are the provinces, there is no way the CBC can adequately reflect the values of individual communities within those regions.
For example, we have the situation in Windsor. Windsor is very much like some isolated communities in the
northern territories. They are isolated in terms of their geography. Now they have basically lost their only Canadian voice, they feel isolated from the larger community of Canada.
The fact is that in Windsor they are essentially awash in American culture. Over 90 per cent of the programming that comes in is American. The only Canadian signal coming in as a local signal was the CBC outlet in Windsor. Now that has been closed their community values are reflected not through a local station, but through a Toronto broadcast.
Whether it be Windsor in the province of Ontario, Saskatchewan, Alberta or British Columbia where the majority of the population on the coast has very different values and views than some of our interior communities, it is impossible for the CBC to reflect those various community values appropriately.

speechtext:
I am pleased to participate in debate on the motion of the member for Mount Royal which reads:
That this House call upon the government as a matter of priority
to ensure that the CBC be strengthened as an instrument of national
identity providing local, regional, and national services to all
Canadians.
May I say in speaking to the motion of the member for Mount Royal that the member has certainly done her colleagues in the the Official Opposition, in the Liberal Party, proud. I believe she has provided a tremendous service to all Canadians concerned about the future of the CBC in the way she has consistently represented them and this issue for such a long period of time in Parliament, in committee and before the CRTC.
The very fact that the member found it necessary today to move this motion really speaks volumes about what is happening in Canada. The motion calls upon the government to ensure that the CBC be strengthened as an instrument of national identity providing local, regional, and national service to all Canadians. The Broadcast Act, both the 1968 act and the new act not yet proclaimed, provide exactly that the CBC ought to have a mandate to provide national, regional, and local service.
March 25, 1991

I am quoting directly from the new act. The words are exactly the same in the old act. They indicate that "the CBC reflect Canada and its regions to national and regional audiences while serving the special needs of those regions". What do the words "special needs"? Who are those special people? What are their special circumstances?
The member who spoke before me talked about Windsor. I agree that Windsor is in a particular situation where its needs are indeed special and important. It is almost isolated, surrounded by that great neighbour of ours, the United States of America. Its connection with the rest of Canada is tenuous, but it is certainly difficult to maintain, particularly when we see the close-down of the CBC station in Windsor.
What about Goose Bay, Labrador, represented by my friend, the member for Labrador? He is the first member for Labrador. An historic position of trust is held by Mr. Rompkey. My friend from Labrador has eloquently told us before the CRTC of the position of the people in Goose Bay, in Churchill Falls, and in Labrador West who occupy a huge sparsely populated land mass and have lost their only vehicle to speak directly to their fellow Newfoundlanders and fellow Canadians. In speaking as he has with such eloquence, the member has reminded us of the special plight of all northern Canadians who need every possible vehicle to speak to their fellow Canadians.
I represent the town of Corner Brook which lost its local station. However, it is not just Comer Brook that has lost a local station. Comer Brook serves an area of some 600 or 700 miles of coast line stretching from Port aux Basques in the south to St. Anthony in the north. It is 600 or 700 miles as the crow flies, in a straight line, but it covers thousands of miles of coast line and hundreds of small isolated communities for whom the CBC is not a luxury. It is not a selection on the channel. It is not a question of taking out the remote and flicking around until something grabs their attention. The CBC is how they find out whether or not they should go out and fish today. It tells them whether the weather is any good, whether they might catch fish or drown in a storm. It is that fundamental. There are no other stations.
Government Orders
The CBC is the only opportunity to speak of the potential and the problems of the people who live in those communities, the people who harvest the sea, who live off the land, who do not wake up in the morning and find six metal boxes containing six national newspapers on their sidewalks, who do not walk down to the drug store and pick up variety of magazines, who do not turn on the radio and go through a selection of Am-FM channels. These are people who turn on their radio and turn on their television and connect to the CBC because the CBC has a mandate to serve them.
The private sector is not there. The private sector is never going to be there, nor should it. There is not a buck to be made. There is not an advertising dollar to be picked up and banked. That is why Parliament mandated the CBC to serve Canadians no matter where they live, no matter what their circumstance.
The greatest irony of all is if we look at the history of the institution. Where did it come from? The notion or the idea of the CBC was born almost 60 years ago. Prime Minister R. B. Bennett, in the middle of the Great Depression in 1931, brought in the Broadcast Act. He understood in the middle of a depression, at a time when the fabric that normally holds a country together is strained, frayed and tom and when the country is having its heart ripped out by the Great Depression, that he needed another instrument to pull this country back together. He envisaged the CBC, and it was bom in the Great Depression of 1931.
In the recession of 1991, what does this Conservative Prime Minister do, this inheritor of R. B. Bennett's mandate? Does he understand the need to pull the country together when the ties that bind are strained?

speechtext: No.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
No, Mr. Speaker. He pulls out a huge pair of fiscal scissors and he severs the last remaining strands of the fabric of this country. He cuts off and isolates the people of Comer Brook, St. Anthony, Coxes Cove, La Scie, White Bay and Hampden. He cuts adrift the people of Windsor. He completely severs the people of Labrador. He closes down Calgary, and he says it is all done in the name of fiscal responsibility.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
This issue is not going away. It is not just about the 11 television stations, the 150 local programs, the 1,100 staff that have been brutally, mindlessly and stupidly cut adrift. That is not what it is about. It is about a visceral understanding deep in the gut of this country that our institutions are being melted down and are vanishing just as the snow vanishes in the spring. Canadians know that if they do not hold on, if they do not stand up now and stop this meltdown of the institutions that define Canada, then Canada will surely follow the fate of the CBC, VTA Rail, Air Canada, and all the other national services that have disappeared.
I come from Newfoundland. I know my province is not as wealthy as some others. I do not envy those who have greater opportunity than mine. I know that we will never be as wealthy as some others, but I have always know that in some ways, in some areas, notwithstanding the disparity of resources, as a Canadian I was equal to any other Canadian.
I have always known that our health care system was there, giving us a measure of equality. I am not sure whether that will be there in a few years. I have always known that in my retirement I would have the dignity of a Canada pension. If all else failed, my country provided that. I have always known that my children and I would have access to quality education; at least I used to think that. I have always known that I could speak to my fellow Canadian. Even though I lived on an island province 19 miles away from the mainland of of Canada, on the east coast of Canada, through the most vicious storm and the thickest fog our voice could cut and be heard because we had a vehicle called the CBC.
We oppose what is happening to the CBC. We believe the CRTC now must be the voice of the people of Canada who do not have the privilege of standing in this Chamber to be heard. The CRTC must say no, just as the people of Canada are saying no to the meltdown of this country. The sooner that Mr. Veilleux and Mr. Watson, who orchestrated the assassination in the dead of night of 1,100 employees and 11 stations, leave the CBC, the sooner the CBC can be better served by new management.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I always enjoy listening to my colleague
from Newfoundland. Ele speaks with great passion, great eloquence and makes a lot of sense.
The kind of passion that we have just heard enunciated in the Chamber by the member from Newfoundland is the very kind of passion that we are seeing pouring forth in support of the CBC by groups that are coming to the CRTC hearings from one end of Canada to the other. People are coming of their own goodwill and expense to defend this institution of public broadcasting and to tell the CRTC in no uncertain terms that it has to do whatever it can to turn this government in its tracks and stop the kind of bludgeoning that is taking place to this institution. Let us stop the kind of emancipation that is taking place and the dismantling of a broadcasting system that is more than a broadcasting system. It is very much, in every part, a tool to help Canadians understand themselves, a tool to help us listen to our own Canadian voices.
I want to ask the member, because he touched very briefly on one aspect of the CBC that I think is extremely important, and that is in our international role. As the member knows, Radio Canada International has had a severe reduction in its funding in the latest round of cuts to the CBC. As a result of that, we have almost another 100 people thrown out on the street. This government loves to throw them out on the street. We have a reduction of foreign programming from 14 languages down to 5.
I just want to ask the member to perhaps reflect on what that is going to do to Canada's international reputation and Canada's voice in the world at large.

-one really has to wonder whether or not the policy of the Minister of Justice, who is speaking across the way, is that Radio Canada International need not exist in the nine languages that are being cut out because the Voice of America is there. I have one other comment for the member. I find it ironic that the former chairman of the CRTC, Mr. Keith Spicer, is now heading up a citizens' forum trying to find out what makes this country sick, angry and upset and what would pull it back together. I want to tell the remaining members of the CRTC, the commissioners now there, that they have within their grasp the ability to excite this country, to turn this country on, to inspire this country in ways that Keith Spicer can only dream about. They can do that by showing the people of Canada that the airwaves truly belong to the people. They do not belong to the NDP, Liberals, Tories, governments or oppositions; they do not belong to the CBC, CTV nor Global. They belong to the people. And the people, somewhere, have a regulator who works for the people, regulating the people's airwaves.
The CRTC can make a statement about Canada, in spite of all the doom and gloom and negative predictions about our future, that shows the people of Canada the system can work. subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it might be appropriate to start a discussion on the CBC with a piece of poetry. The lines that I have in mind are from The Merchant of Venice where Shylock says: "You take my house when you take the prop that sustains my house". There are scholars in the Elouse who will correct me if I am wrong, but my recollection is that is what he says: "You take my house when you take the prop that sustains my house."
It is appropriate because that is exactly what the CBC is. It is the prop that sustains our house. It is appropriate to use a little poetry because we should not underesti-
Government Orders
mate the contribution of the CBC to the arts in this country. Gordon Pinsent, who is a famous Canadian actor now and a famous international actor, came from my province. Would he be where he is today had it not been for the CBC? Would shows like Codco be on the air? Would troops like the Mummers have grown up? Would drama reflecting the soul of my province be as alive as it is today without the CBC? The answer is clearly no.
That is why it is appropriate to start the discussion with that particular quotation. It seems to me it is the prop that sustains this House. The government may do away with the railway. We never had a railway in Labrador so we are not going to miss it. The government may do away with Petro-Canada, but we will find other oil companies to develop the oil and the gas off our coasts. The government may do away with the post office, and that will make a difference to us. It will make it tough for us, but we will survive. We will be the same as we are without the post office.
But when you tamper with the CBC, you tamper with the last fundamental unifying force in this country. The CBC is the way we talk to each other. The CBC is the way we communicate. This government is responsible for tampering with, and starting to dismantle by atrophy, the last unifying force in this country.
Mr. Watson tells us that he uses this occasion of a budget cut to create a new vision for the CBC. His vision is a window, a regional window whereby Canadians talk to each other. They see through that window and they talk to each other. That is Mr. Watson's new vision. Mr. Watson robs us of our window in the north in order to create his new regional vision.
That is exactly what the CBC was. It was a window that reflected us to ourselves, that told us about each other, a way we talked to each other at the local level. It was also a window through which we expressed ourselves to the rest of Canada and hopefully to the world, but certainly to the rest of Canada.
In creating his new window, he has robbed us of what made us unique, that unique possibility for expression and communication because, as my hon. friend from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte has said so eloquently: "There is no option for us". The private sector does not exist in Labrador. There are no private stations. Why? Because there is no market for them. There is no money to be made.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
All the signals we get are from satellites. All the signals we get are sitcoms from the United States and elsewhere. There is no other local vehicle except the CBC.
In the north it is important now that we be able to talk back to the south, to those signals that come to us from the south. If we do not, we are going to be inundated by those signals, swamped by those signals and whatever culture and whatever identity we have will be submerged and eventually destroyed unless we have some way of talking back.
If you think, Mr. Speaker, there are solitudes in this country, and that they are east and west, and that they are French and English, I will tell you about other solitudes. They are north and south. The north believes that the south does not understand what it is all about, that it is on the margin, that it is not important, that it is out there and not really fundamentally part of this country. At a time in the history of this country when there are forces at work tearing us apart, it is essential more so than ever before that we have a local means of making our voice heard in this national debate.
That is what the CBC is all about. If the 30,000 people I represent were here today, they would say the same thing. Not just me; the mayor of Fermont, which is our sister community across the border in Quebec, was at the CRTC hearing the morning before I was there. He said exactly the same thing. If the mayor of Sept-Iles was here, he would say the same thing.
It does not really matter. We are not unique in Labrador except that we are part of the north, except that we are on the margin, except that we need that voice, the voice that CBC was for us. That is why this is so important. We have depended on the CBC.
Let me give credit where credit is due. The CBC, certainly as far as radio is concerned, has been a unifying factor and has reflected our local reality. We cannot say the same for CBC television.
I understand that camera crews have been on the coast of Labrador doing set pieces: a piece on alcoholism,
another piece that can be shown at any time that they can slip in for 10 or 15 minutes to reflect that particular part of Canada. But that is not the local day-to-day reality of the Labrador coast. It is the difference between the play-by-play of Bob Cole and the Hot Stove League between periods.
We want the local day-by-day reality reflected in this country now, and that is what CBC region has not done up to now. The track record is not there for us. My people in Labrador know more about what is going on in the St. John's city council than they do about the Goose Bay town council or the Labrador City town council.
The stations at Goose Bay and Labrador City reflected that local reality, created a way whereby people could talk to each other and created a way whereby those Canadians could talk to their counterparts in the south in this debate.
The money saved is minimal. The jobs lost are minimal compared to the importance of those stations to us. As my colleague from Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte has said, it is now up to the CRTC as the final court of appeal in the country to recognize the reality of those local stations. As our colleague from Winnipeg said so eloquently and so passionately the other day, the regional vision of Mr. Watson is not going to reach deep into the roots of this country, is not going to reflect the heart and soul of rural Canada, of small town Canada, of northern Canada. Only those local stations could do that.
It is now up to the CRTC, and I hope that this House will reflect it, up to the CRTC to rule that we must not tamper with what is the last and greatest unifying force in this country. We can only hope, and the people who I represent can only hope that the CRTC will recognize that and rule accordingly. If they do not we will have lost out in this great national debate.
