speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I jotted down some rules because I wanted to speak to this motion moved by the Hon. Member for Mount Royal.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
I could not leave unanswered the absurd statements made by the Hon. Member for Labrador as well as the Hon. Member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte. When listening to the Hon. Member for Labrador, one gets the impression that people in Newfoundland and Labrador have no access to television service in this country. Such is not the case, Mr. Speaker, because on the basis of the statistics in our possession, which by the way are available to any one, 99 per cent of the people in Labrador and Newfoundland own a television set. Well, if 99 per cent of people in Newfoundland and Labrador have their own television sets, Mr. Speaker, they must certainly watch television programming. It is quite untrue and unacceptable to be told today in the House that Newfoundlanders are at a disadvantage by comparison with other Canadians.
We understand that it is this Parliament's duty to provide free and equal access without charge to all Canadians, even those in some remote areas. We understand that. However, Mr. Speaker, our colleagues from Newfoundland are telling us they are at a disadvantage in comparison with other Canadians as far as television programming is concerned. Nevertheless, Mr. Speaker, when you look at the statistics compiled by the CBC, it is strange to see that nowadays in Newfoundland, not only in St. John's, but throughout the province, and even in small municipalities, 64 per cent of households have cable TV. That figure is pretty considerable. Besides the basic service everyone-that is 99 per cent of the people-can get with an antenna, 64 per cent of households in that province also have cable TV. That is more than in Prince Edward Island, where only 48 per cent have cable TV than in New Brunswick, and even than in Quebec with 59 per cent.
So if the hon. member for Humber-St. Barbe-Baie Verte thought he could move us to tears today, he was dead wrong, Mr. Speaker, because with these options, he has access to all the TV stations and radio channels the people in Newfoundland, just like people all over Canada, can choose from.
Mr. Speaker, in this debate proposed by the hon. member for Mount Royal, her colleagues in the Liberal Party and also to some extent in the New Democratic Party have painted a picture which is all black. They tried
to tell us that the last chance to save Canadian unity was to add to the $1.4 billion we already give to the CBC.
However, when you look at the figures, and we must, Mr. Speaker, since we need to back up what we say. One should not throw words which have more to do with paranoia than anything else. There is a lot of paranoia in the opposition, but arguments must be based on facts.
The hon. member told us a while ago that the last instrument to save national unity was the CBC. Watching "The National" and "The Journal" was the thing to do. If we don't watch those, Canada can't be saved. Then, Mr. Speaker, what could my friend from Labrador say about the TV watching habits of English-speaking Canadians.
Let us look, for example, at the results of the latest poll conducted by BBM, in the Fall of 1988, on the TV watching habits of English-speaking Canadians. Some 25.8 per cent of their viewing-time was devoted to the English Canadian network CTV; 26 per cent, to English Canadian independant stations; 28 per cent, to the American broadcasting stations, and 18 per cent, to the English CBC.
Mr. Speaker, does that mean, according to what the Liberal members are saying, that for 82 per cent of the time spent watching TV in English Canada, people do not contribute to the national unity? That would mean that most of the time, 82 per cent of the time people in Vancouver, in Montreal or in Saint John's watch an English broadcasting station other than CBC and they are not contributing to the national unity.
I think we have been presented with a false debate today and I find most regrettable that attempts are being made now to make political propaganda or partisan politics out of the current situation of the CBC. It is a fact that we have had to make the best of past mistakes for which we were not responsible. In 1984, our government inherited a debt that all of us, as Canadians, will have to pay for a long time to come.
That problem cannot be settled in 5, 6, 7 or 10 years. We have taken actions that will allow for a gradual reduction of our national debt over the next several years. However, one important thing must be said to the Canadian population. This year alone, Canadian taxpayers across the land will spend 1.4 billion dollars to allow CBC to maintain its radio and television services in French and in English.
March 25, 1991

It is, a considerable amount of money. As for me, what makes me angry when I hear Liberal members in particular speak on this matter, it is that we have the impression that in Canada there is only Radio-Canada and the CBC. What about the rest? How many times have liberal members stood in the House to speak of the problems plaguing private television stations in Canada, Mr. Speaker?
In my constituency of Shawinigan, people can listen every day to programs on their radio or television, a fact which contradicts what our colleagues opposite say, that our radio and television in Canada is pityful, of poor quality, and that it is not diversified.
Shawinigan is a town of 23,000 inhabitants. A small town similar to others across the country. Every day, the people of Shawinigan can tune in 29 FM radio stations, on cable, in French and English. Not bad for a small town of 23,000. And when they have had enough of radio, because people in Quebec listen to 15 hours of radio weekly, they switch to their favorite hobby, television. Quebecers watch 27 hours of television per week; half the time, they watch programs on CBC. But if the people of Shawinigan or other small towns in Canada can tune in to 29 radio stations on cable-
Mr. Speaker, the people of Shawinigan can also tune in to a grand total of 33 TV stations, a pretty fair choice I would suggest.
I wish one NDP or one Liberal member on the other side of this House would point to one country in the world with a small population of 27 million as we are in Canada, including 7 million in Quebec, where TV viewers and radio listeners have access to such a wide variety of means of communications.
Last November, Mr. Speaker, I went to Belgium, which happens to be a fairly important country in Europe. I turned on the TV and began searching for stations. As I just said a moment ago, cable TV in Shawinigan enables the wiewer to choose among 33 stations, a good selection. As people are wont to do, I began zapping to locate other stations. Well, I got the two stations in Belgium, the RTBF1 network and the RTBF2 network.
Now over to France, Mr. Speaker. Switch on the TV. In terms of population, France is bigger than either Quebec or Canada. You turn on the TV and get

Mr. Speaker, the CBC alone has 1,600 antennas from coast to coast for French and English TV and radio broadcasting.
These media provide us with information services that are second to none. Of course the CBC network is not the only choice we have to get the good and the bad news. To inform us of all the radio broadcasting services available to us.

Having said that, Mr. Speaker, all Hon. Members agree-we clearly said so when dealing with Bill C-40 with which I was very actively involved by moving a number of amendments-that the CBC has a vital and very important role to play.
Mr. Speaker, the government is well aware of that. That is why we raise through taxes in my riding and the whole country a considerable amount of money which is used for only part of our broadcasting system. For the CBC, which is just one element in our system, we raise $1.4 billion in Canada.

It is enough and, Mr. Speaker, considering the economic situation, the CBC has a duty to spend this money wisely, because I think those people in the CBC tower on Dorchester in Montreal-excuse me, on Rene Levesque Boulevard-should remember one thing: They are spending taxpayers' money.
The other issue, Mr. Speaker, is that the CBC is competing unfairly with the private sector, especially in Quebec but also in English Canada.

Mr. Speaker, I would also like to talk very briefly about RCI, our short wave international service. Many Canadians do not know exactly what it is. RCI is Canada's voice abroad which allows millions of listeners in Europe, in Asia, in Africa and in the Middle East to hear from Canada. We expect that the government will soon tell us what it intends to do exactly with this service. The Opposition has already mentioned some further cuts. It is possible, Mr. Speaker, that there may be some cuts. I will probably be the first one to regret it because I think the Canadian government must provide an international
short wave service through RCI which is accessible to the largest possible number of people throughout the world.
However, Mr Speaker, we must also acknowledge the fact that Canada is not the only country in the world reviewing its policy with regard to short wave radio service. Radio-Australia is in the process of doing so and so are Radio-Denmark, Radio-Sweden, Radio-Finland. Radio-4 in Belgium is cutting its short wave international service level and is even thinking of doing away with it altogether. RSA, the voice of South Africa, has cut the bulk of its services in French and in English to North America. Radio-Prague, in Czechoslovakia, is in the process of redefining its services as a whole. Why, Mr. Speaker? Because, unfortunately, shortwaves are no longer the modern way of communicating.
Of course, I really think we must keep some shortwave services. Russia, for example. For my part, I wholeheartedly wish the government will maintain our service in the Russian language, because there is one thing we must aknowledge, Radio-Canada International is not listened by only a few hundred listeners in the Soviet Union. In fact, Radio Canada International has a higher rating in the Soviet Union than the CBC here in Canada, which shows how important that service is to us.
Last year, Mr. Speaker, 7,460,000 Soviet citizens listened to Radio Canada International. I believe it is a useful service, and I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs to maintain Russian language broadcasting which represent a very important part of RCI's activities. According to a 1987 survey, Mr. Speaker, Radio Canada International had 16 millions listeners around the world. Maybe, in a few days, we will not be able to serve all the international community. However, considering the importance of the Russian broadcasting for the Soviet Union, I really wish it be maintained.
Also, Mr. Speaker, we must recognize that the CBC International German broadcasting for West Germany and East Germany is listened to by only 50 000 people. I wonder why we are still providing this service. If there is a service that should be cut given our priorities, it is that one. However, Mr. Speaker, I think we must keep and even improve our Spanish broadcasting which is widely listened to in Cuba.

During a trip to Cuba, a few years ago, I met many Cubans whose only source of information coming from North America was Radio Canada International, for its waves are very well received in Havana. That is a service which, Mr. Speaker, I think we should maintain. On the other hand, other short wave services could be dropped, or revised as most other average countries like Canada have done-I have mentioned these countries just before-before cutting or reducing the whole of their short wave services.
Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to say to my friend from Mount Royal that her motion, as interesting as it might be, does not reflect the reality, because this government will continue to invest large amounts in its public broadcasting system, and Canadians will still choose between a public and a private system, because we can afford both.
For my part and in the opinion of my constituents, from my riding of Saint-Maurice, I must say, Mr. Speaker, that $1.4 billion represent a appropriate sum which we committed ourselves to maintain this year. I am sure that CBC management will know how to spend that money discreetly while securing the linguistic duality the federal government wishes to maintain and ensuring that official language minorities, anglophone everywhere in Quebec and francophone outside Quebec, will obtain a better service.
This is the rule we applied during the last few years, Mr. Speaker. The English-speaking minority in the Mauricie, Trois-Rivieres and Shawinigan area did not have, when Liberals were in power, a local relay for the signals originating in Montreal, Quebec City and Toronto. Now they have. A whole series of French-speaking communities outside Quebec did not have this service. Since 1984, we have worked to give Canadians, from both language groups, access to these services. Our work is not over yet, Mr. Speaker, but we will keep at it. I am sure that Canadian citizens know that we are using their tax money with the utmost prudence and that we try to protect the high quality and reputation of the CBC, renowned around the world.

The privatization of Petro-Canada, cutbacks to VIA Rail, closure of rural post offices, privatization of Air Canada, the free trade agreement, the watering down of CBC's role in the development of our national identity have all chipped away at these national institutions that were such an important element in our cultural and practical Canadian way of life. As a result of this government's lack of financial support for the CBC, the CBC was forced to cut back. In cutting back, regional coverage was made to suffer, in addition to a number of other important services.
In my area in eastern Canada a very important element of our culture was brought to an end. For 20 years eastern Canadians watched the program Land and Sea. This show provided eastern Canadians with a reflection of the people, the activities and the culture of the Atlantic area. The program gave the dairy farmer in Malpeque an understanding of the way of life and the problems of the lobster fishermen. It provided the tourist operator an opportunity to comprehend the needs and concerns of the potato farmer. It gave all islanders an outlet to enjoy and understand the diverse priorities that exist in our region of the country.
The dropping of the program Land and Sea has reduced the ability of eastern Canadians to understand ourselves, our identity and our differences and similarities.

Mr. Speaker, the member has made some rather provocative statements here today. One of the comments he made earlier in his presentation was that the CBC should be essentially chastized for going more and more into the commercial market for what he calls unfair competition with private broadcasters in Canada.
I just want to point out to the member that he cannot have it both ways. The fact is that the CBC has had to go more and more into commercial revenues because this government has cut back more and more of its public revenues.
If the corporation were facing fixed costs as any business enterprise does-it faces fixed or increasing costs year after year as inflation takes place-it has to make up that funding somewhere. If it cannot get it from the government, if it cannot get it from the public purse, then it will have to raise those revenues through competition in the commercial field.
I say to the member that he cannot have it both ways. He is complaining that this unfair competition is happening when his government is the very culprit that is forcing the CBC to rely more and more heavily on those commercial revenues.

We find 1,100 people turfed out on the street, 11 regional broadcast centres closed, the cutting of over 140 programs, and the CBC facing another budget cut of $50 million to $60 million and another 500 jobs on the line.

Mr. Speaker, may I first of all request the indulgence of the House to share my time with my learned colleague from Edmonton Southeast.

Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to take part in this debate this afternoon. First, I would like to congratulate my colleague the hon. member for Mount Royal who moved the motion to which I bring the attention of the House:
That this House call upon the Government as a matter of priority to
ensure that the CBC be strenghtened as an instrument of national
identity providing local, regional, and national services to all
Canadians.
This motion, Mr. Speaker, deserves our support, in fact, the unanimous support of the House of Commons. At the beginning of the proceedings today, at one o'clock, I think, the House was presented with the report of the Commissioner of Official Languages. Mr. D'Iberville Fortier, the Commissioner of Official Languages, who is not an Opposition member nor a NDP member nor a partisan of any sort but rather a servant of this House, precisely says in his report concerning CBC- and I call to your attention, Mr. Speaker, what is said on page 20 of the English version: "In spite of the brave front put on by CBC executives, it is hard to believe that the Corporation will be able to fulfill its current basic mandate. Canadian identity, we fear, cannot be promoted by showing "Dallas" and "L.A. Law" in English and French. The CBC must have a strong national and regional presence. Regional programming has been slashed to such a point that it may never recover".
This is what Mr. D'Iberville Fortier, the Commissioner of Official languages, says in his report tabled here in this House, already a few hours ago.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
In the recommendations contained in Mr. Fortier's report, on page 65, we can read the following about broadcasting and more particurlarly about television: "A recommendation to the CRTC on improved access by minorities to broadcasts of House of Commons debates."
Here is the next recommendation: "A recommendation to the CBC on improved services to minority language communities. Result: not implemented. Situation in 1991 will likely be considerably worse than in 1988 because of budget cuts."
This is what the Commissioner of Official languages had to say about this government's broadcasting policy, a government which has cut funding to the CBC and forcing it to reduce its local and regional programming.
Mr. Speaker, the hon. member for Saint-Maurice told us earlier-and I can see him in the House-about the cuts to CBC's funding and he was saying, and I want to make sure I am quoting him accurately, that in Canada we also have private broadcasters and that we should talk about them. I did not have the opportunity earlier to ask questions to my colleague from Saint-Maurice, but I still want to remind him that outside Quebec, there is no private French television station in all of Canada. Not one, Mr. Speaker. Francophones outside Quebec have either access to Radio-Canada services or none at all. As people from Glengarry-Prescott-Russell would say: "We ain't have any." And that's that.
So, as Francophones outside Quebec, we need this tool to preserve our cultural identity and our language, Mr. Speaker.
We talk about local programming. Mr. Speaker, let me give you some examples of what is happening in Ontario. We have the television station CBOFT, in Ottawa, of course, and there is another CBC television station, in Toronto, CBLFT, which serves the greater Toronto, and then one station for Northern Ontario. Now, CBOFT serves the Ottawa-Hull area. CBC has announced that from now on programming in French for all of Ontario would be done out of Ottawa. When Mr. Gougeon, of the CBC, testified before the Standing Committee on Communications and Culture, on December 11, 1990, I asked him how they would serve the people in those
areas. Or rather it was Mr. Veilleux I had the opportunity to question.
So, before this Parliamentary Committee, Mr. Veilleux answered: "You know, we will serve the people in Ontario through our station in Ottawa." So, I said: "All right." So if that is what they do, how are they going to serve western Quebec, Mr. Veilleux, because right now we have the news-or we had the news-from Ottawa-Hull on the CBC". Here is what he said: "Hull and western Quebec will be served from Montreal". "Fair enough, I said, but how? There is no broadcasting antenna. You will need another antenna if you want all that". From Hull you cannot directly tune in a station from Montreal; it cannot be done, unless of course they are directly linked by cable. Otherwise it does not work, we are out of range, the two cities are 100 miles apart, or 160 kilometres. There is no way to tune in directly. To that he replied: "We can review our plans to see what can be done to serve both audiences".
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, the people in Timmins would hear all about a traffic jam in Gatineau. Imagine what that would do, how logical it would be to have that kind of programming. The CBC management insist on the fact that they now serve a region instead of a locality. They even have a rather loose interpretation of the word "region". For instance, Hawkesbury, in my riding, and Kakabeka Falls, along the Manitoba border, are part of the same region according to CBC. Mr. Speaker, it is like saying-if we transpose that to United States for a moment-that New York, Denver and Atlanta are part of the same region. Distances are almost the same. Hawkesbury is almost as far from Orlando, Florida, as from Kakabeka Falls, Ontario. And yet, they are considered to be in the same region. What do they have in common for programming, Mr. Speaker? Not much, and that kind of programming is not possible. People will get bad services.
Ontario is not the only region to suffer from CBC cuts.
I myself welcome young students from the Embrun Secondary School who are visiting Parliament today. These young people know, for example, how important it is to have programs like Genies en Herbe, Smac, Tele-Relais, L'Acadie and other programs produced by CBC. Of course, everything is cut now.
March 25, 1991

I see the Secretary of State is here, in the House, now, Mr. Speaker. He is a man I rather appreciate and I would like to remind him that he is responsible for linguistic minorities in Canada-as he knows well-and tell him that I trust he will convince his colleagues to do something in order to ensure that CBC maintains its local programming to serve French speaking minorities in Canada, the French speaking Canadians outside Quebec. I agree with Mr. Rolland Beaulieu, the New Brunswick minister who, appearing before the CRTC a while ago, declared that CBC and the federal government must act to correct an unfair situation which leaves Acadians defenceless against assimilation and endangers their very existence.

Mr. Speaker, a greater unity is essential if we are going to survive as a single great nation.
A CBC which respects its regional mandate-I am not saying that it does that now as well as it should-could be a major unifying vehicle to allow all Canadians equally, without regional favourites, to share a cultural heritage which reflects our full national identity.
Those opposite, some of whom detest the CBC, clearly have it in their sights as a candidate for dismantling by denying it funds, or oxygen, as they have done with VIA Rail and other national institutions in the past.
If we can judge from news reports over the weekend, the government wants us to increase defence spending. The headline in one paper today is "Tories Urge Big Increase in Spending on Military."
By the way, the Minister of Transport will know that $13 billion is already being spent on defence in this country. Some of us think that that is not the priority to keep this country together.
The new Broadcasting Act says that the programming provided by the CBC should "reflect Canada and its regions to the national regional audiences while serving the special needs of those regions".
CBC cuts have resulted in the closing of three local television stations, downsizing eight others and cancelling hundreds of hours per year of programs, particularly in local and regional television, thus shutting off the
voice input of many of our regions of Canada. It has become impossible for the CBC regions to fulfil their mandate, to reflect the regions to themselves and to one another.
I do not think the CBC is doing well enough in this regional mandate and what is happening now is just going to make it harder. Fil Fraser of Edmonton, the former CBC broadcaster and a member of the Spicer commission has described the CBC regions in the past as "a sham". "The regions are not producing programs because they have no access to the network schedules, and they do not have any money to produce with." What was true several years ago when Mr. Fraser said that is undoubtedly more true today.
There seems to be no end in sight for the CBC's budget cuts as the corporation expects a further shortfall in annual operating resources of almost $50 million by fiscal year 1992-93. The foreseeable strategy for the corporation's survival should be, presumably, further cuts to regional programming.
I might indicate that a friend of mine who works for the CBC tells me that CBC stereo is expected to be the next thing to be cut by this so-called government opposite. It that happens, some of us who listen to it will feel that we have lost a very close friend.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the motion before us today is one which touches the daily lives of virtually every Canadian. It asks that the national broadcaster of Canada, the CBC, and I quote from the motion: "be strengthened as an instrument of national identity providing local, regional, and national services to all Canadians".
Quite frankly, I am surprised that the members would want to bring this up again today after all of the discussion we have had over the last four months. Actually, we have been debating this particular matter for a number of years. I guess there may be some connection to the fact that there is a lobby group that is meeting here in the House this afternoon. That is probably why the opposition benches are virtually empty as well. There are probably a lot of people over there. That may be the reason, and I do not know if it is a very substantive reason, for bringing this kind of debate up here in the House.
I thought it was important to talk about the mandate that has been given to the CBC and in fact to all the broadcasters in this new legislation. We have heard a lot of rhetoric about what is going on, but I think it is important that we discuss the actual facts.
I think we should also look at the process that has gone through since 1985 when a task force on the future of broadcasting in Canada reported right through until February 1, 1991, when Royal Assent was given.
This long, exhaustive process has had as its raison d'etre the shape of our broadcasting system, and the CBC's role within it. The 1985 report of the task force recognized the vital role that the CBC plays in the lives of all Canadians, but suggested that its activities could be more

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
focused. The government's response to that suggestion was very positive. It acted on a number of recommendations to focus the CBC's mandate on its Canadian contributions.
A new broadcasting policy was put in place in June 1988. It recognized that the CBC was the cornerstone of the Canadian broadcasting system. At the same time, it recognized that the corporation was no longer the only broadcaster. Therefore, its mandate was focused toward reflecting Canada to its audience, and to being predominantly and distinctively Canadian.
That legislation died in the other place when the election of 1988 was called, but new legislation was introduced in 1989. Following extensive parliamentary committee hearings, where the hon. member for Mount Royal played an important and influential role, the bill finally received Royal Assent seven weeks ago.
The question of the role of the CBC has been in the public eye for nearly six years. It has been under examination in Parliament more or less continuously for the past three.
I would respectfully submit that the passage of this important legislation reflects in the strongest possible way this government's commitment to Canadian broadcasting, programming and to the renewal of a vital and meaningful public broadcaster. This new legislation will come into force in the near future.
I think it is appropriate to very quickly point out the important mandate which this legislation places on the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Recognizing the enormous contribution of public broadcasting to the creation and exhibition of all forms of Canadian programming, this new Broadcasting Act reaffirms in strong and clear terms the role of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation as the primary instrument of broadcasting and cultural policy in Canada.
Time and time again, this government has reiterated its primary policy objective in introducing and passing new broadcasting legislation which will make more and better Canadian programs accessible to all Canadians.
The new Broadcasting Act makes it clear that the CBC is vital in this enterprise. Indeed, it redefines the mandate of the CBC to permit it to better concentrate
on this activity. For the first time, it recognizes that other Canadian broadcasters should do their fair share to contribute to a vital Canadian programming industry as well.
The new Broadcasting Act builds this Canadian programming strategy around the CBC. There is absolutely no doubt that the CBC will continue to play its central role as the national broadcaster.
The new Broadcasting Act ensures that the CBC will remain the principal vehicle for cultural expression in Canada. It will continue to serve Canadians by providing a distinctly Canadian viewpoint and a broad range of programming, including news, variety, drama and sports.
The mandate of the CBC as contained in the new act expects the CBC to continue to lead in providing authentically Canadian choices, particularly in popular drama in both official languages. By tradition the CBC has enjoyed an arm's length relationship with the government. In fact, for the first time the CBC's freedom of expression and its journalistic and programming independence are clearly stated in the legislation.
As the national public broadcaster, the CBC is and will remain under the new Broadcasting Act a strong and independent voice and the foremost producer of Canadian radio and television programming.
The new Broadcasting Act reformulates the CBC's mandate to place greater emphasis on the distinctly Canadian character of CBC programming. For the first time this mandate includes specific references to the important role that the CBC performs in reflecting Canada and its regions to national and regional audiences, in providing English and French programming services, in meeting the needs of official language minorities, in reflecting Canadian society in all its aspects, in actively contributing to the flow and exchange of cultural expression; and in all these ways contributing to a shared national consciousness and identity.
Critics have lamented the removal of the phrase "national unity" from the CBC's mandate. Yet there can be no doubt that the objectives, which I have just cited, will indeed contribute to Canadian unity. But how can there be unity without the flow and exchange of cultural expression in English and in French among all regions of Canada? How can there be unity without a shared national consciousness and identity?
March 25, 1991

The new Broadcasting Act reinterprets the objective of Canadian unity, now in the CBC's mandate, in terms which are more appropriate to a truly independent public broadcaster. The CBC's mandate is refocused to emphasize that its programming should be predominantly and distinctively Canadian, reflecting Canada and its regions to national and regional audiences.
The mandate of the CBC as contained in this new Broadcasting Act expects the CBC to continue to lead in providing authentically Canadian programming choices in both official languages. At the same time, the new act introduces measures governing the corporation's operations and its financial and administrative accountability to government and to Parliament.
It rationalizes the CBC management structure by separating the very different functions of president and chief executive officer from those of the chairman of the board of directors. This division of responsibilities is consistent with the practices that take place in large corporations and dynamic businesses in the world in which we live today. In fact, it is a change which is long overdue.
The chairman is responsible with the board of directors for establishing broad policies and direction, whereas the president is responsible for the day-to-day management of the corporation within the framework established by the board of directors. Both functions are essential and the positions are complementary.
Mr. Watson and Mr. Veilleux have demonstrated their ability to work well together to provide the CBC with the essential combination of creative vision and sound management which a corporation of its mandate and its scale of operations needs and deserves.
Consistent with the new act's recognition that French and English language broadcasting operate under different conditions, and in fact may have different requirements, the new act establishes standing committees of the CBC board of directors to deal with matters related to French and English language broadcasting. The committees will both be headed by the chairman and the president of the CBC so that those committees can discuss different ideas and different programming and different mandates within the over-all mandate of the
Government Orders
CBC to encourage exchange of ideas between English programming and French programming.
The new act clarifies the nature of the CBC's accountability to Parliament by bringing under the Broadcasting Act measures previously found in other legislation.
It is abundantly clear, by these actions, enshrined in this legislation that the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation is a vital instrument of Canada's national identity. Its mandate is a strong, clear declaration by Parliament. The mandate is realistic, having been crafted and defined in today's circumstances, both within the broadcasting industry and for the country as a whole.
I would like for a moment to address the notion that national identity can only be preserved by the CBC providing local community services as well as regional and national services. I want to talk about the local service just for a moment.
The new act recognizes that the CBC is but one voice in many. Everywhere in this land there are other Canadian broadcasters and other choices. Clearly, the CBC does not need to nor in fact should it try to provide every conceivable service in broadcasting. There are other methods of doing this. There are private broadcasters who provide excellent services. They operate at the local level in their own towns and their own communities to provide the service to their individual communities as they see fit.
It may be that the CBC should not try to duplicate already strong local services, but use its resources to fill its legislated national and regional responsibilities.
As members well know, the CBC provides local, regional and national radio service complemented by regional, national and international television service.
In closing, I would like to place on the record the specific mandate of the CBC as contained in the new Broadcasting Act. I believe members will find it provides for a vibrant and meaningful CBC for the coming decade and beyond. It requires that the CBC, as the national public broadcaster, should provide radio and television services incorporating a wide range of programming that informs, enlightens and entertains.

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
The programming provided by the corporation should be predominantly and distinctively Canadian. It should reflect Canada and its regions to national and regional audiences, while serving the special needs of those regions. It should actively contribute to the flow and exchange of cultural expression, in English and in French, reflecting the different needs and circumstances of each official language community, including the particular needs and circumstances of English and French linguistic minorities. It should strive to be of an equivalent quality in both English and in French. It should contribute to the shared national consciousness and identity. It should be made available throughout Canada by the most appropriate and efficient means and as resources become available for that purpose. It should reflect the multicultural and multiracial nature of Canada.
This mandate for our national broadcaster, the CBC, is unequivocal as to the important role of the CBC in providing programming which will contribute to our shared consciousness of who we are as Canadians, of where we are going and what being Canadian means.
The government is confident that CBC is better equipped today to fulfil this important role. The concerns expressed in this motion, I submit, are unfounded. The new Broadcasting Act gives the corporation both a streamlined mandate and a new corporate structure, both of which will permit the CBC to fulfil its important role in reflecting the Canadian national identity from one coast to the other.

We are debating the question of the CBC and its role as a national broadcaster. We are also discussing the cuts that have occurred at least twice in the last two years. As a consequence of those cuts, the whole question as to whether the CBC is still considered by this government to be a national broadcasting agency is very much a moot point. The original intention of the CBC to provide communications from sea to sea to sea and to permit all of us in Canada, this vast disparate land, to understand a little bit through listening to radio or through watching television about how other people in other regions live. This is somewhat in doubt with these cuts.
I look at the cuts that have occurred in my own region in the last two years. I find it very difficult to convince myself that somebody up there thinks that we are still part of Canada. The food show has been cut. Agricultural reporting during the noon hour has been cut back dramatically. A number of well-known programs in the Atlantic region and sometimes broadcast nationally were cut such as the Land and Sea program. Country Canada is still going but how much longer? As well the farm business news which was aired on the news channel has now been cut after a very successful run of some 16 months.
It makes us wonder just where the commitment went for CBC. We are finding that there are cuts right across the country. Out of Saskatoon the TV channel there has been taken off the air with these cuts. This means that stories which emanate from Saskatchewan that might be picked up on the national feed no longer have a place to come from except out of Regina. I do not know whether all members of the government realize that Saskatchewan is 700 or 800 miles from end to end. It is pretty hard for one station in the very southern part of the province to cover all of that territory. Saskatoon had a chance of making it possible.
I have a list here in my hand of CBC programs cut in British Columbia, Saskatchewan and Manitoba, and it goes on. There must be 23 or 24 programs that have been cut, some of which were heard nationally.
The cuts have been there. They have been real. They have been progressive. What about the cuts that were made a year ago? We were told by the president of CBC, in defending those cuts, that we still had a lot of regionally programming and a lot of resource programming. We were complaining at that time about the imminent departure of George Price who was a fixture around Parliament Hill and came into everyone's living rooms and kitchens at noon across the country. That voice is now dead. There is nobody reporting on food, agriculture and resource matters from Ottawa to the rest of the country.
Some government members and people at CBC who are defending the cuts say that this is simply taking away ghetto broadcasting. Was the food show a ghetto broadcast show? They are arguing that only a few hundred thousand farmers were interested in the food show, yet the main audience for the food show were consumers. Don't we need food? That is the new authority being granted to the CBC: if it is only as universal as food, it is not important.
How far do we carry this kind of thinking? The most popular show on CBC television at the moment is the news show-The National and The Journal-which takes an hour every night. It has very high ratings. Most of the people who are reported on those shows are some 295 people sitting in this Chamber. They take most of the coverage out of that hour every night. They said that
March 25, 1991

they have been told to cut broadcasting because there are only a few hundred thousand farmers left and there are only 26 million consumers in this country who are not interested in food. Yet a program that basically places forward the names and faces of some, if not all, of the 295 people in this Chamber still continues to get plenty of coverage. I suspect that that would be, from this government's point of view, one of the last places that cuts would be proposed. It is just a question of whose ox is being gored, I suppose.
I have mentioned the various cuts that have occurred. They were step by step. We were told when George Price went that we still had programs like Country Canada and the video programs and the all-news program. In fact, one of the quotations from a letter received almost a year ago, April 6, 1990, from the president of CBC defending the cuts that the government had forced on him at that point, justified laying off Mr. Price not because he was being retired, but by not filling the position. He said this was because there were changes, that times change and that it was time that particular show and format disappeared. He wrote: "Today only a very small percentage of CBC's audience claims farming as an occupation. These farmers get up to the minute information from computers, fax, wire services, all-news television and a variety of other sources, as well as CBC Radio".
Since that time, since this last round of cuts, we can forget about all-news television as one of the sources for farm information because that was one of the things that went this time. Farm Business News which was produced in Regina by Agcom Productions aired its last episode last February 16. It was part of the Newsworld operation. It was the only western and agricultural show that appeared on CBC affiliates and channels. It was on the all-news channel and has now disappeared.
I do not think it is just an accident that the shows being pulled not only represent agriculture, the land and the sea, but they were also produced in the regions. That regional ability to employ technicians, producers, writers and broadcasters is now disappearing.
It is more than just losing the service. It is a question of losing the technical ability in those regions to produce this kind of programming either in CBC or outside CBC.
Government Orders
By pulling away this financing and this ability to hold the nation together and to provide the kind of expertise at the regional level, the country is going to be much poorer for it. I think we have lost far more than we are saving with these cuts.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the beginning of my friend's remarks, he made it sound as though we were presiding over the demise of CBC because of the $100 million cutback. I am sure he is aware that the total budget of the CBC is $1.4 billion and that every year it gets bigger.
I would like to ask my friend from Saskatchewan-and his farming community knows a lot about cutting back, where it has to be done-how he would project that in a budget of $1.4 billion a cutback of $100 million would bring about the demise of that corporation.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is the second of those types of cutbacks. It is becoming a habit. If it were only going to be a one-time shot, I am sure CBC could adjust. But each year it makes the cuts, lays off the people and closes the stations. Then it finds at the end of the year that it was not good enough and that it has to do it again the following year.
That is not the way this government has been operating in other areas. It has not had this kind of cutting back in crucial departments. In fact it has been increasing the expenditures in most departments.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Solicitor General of Canada
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext: Would you repeat that?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
We have not seen these kinds of cutbacks in departmental expenditures. The expenditures of this government now are much higher than they were when it took office. They have gone up each of those years. The deficit has gone up. The expenditures have gone up. Expenditures have not been brought down on a continuous curve, the same way that the CBC has been asked to make its cuts in the last couple of years.
If there was an assurance that these were the last cuts, I am sure the country and CBC could make adjustments. They had a cut last year. Then they got this year's cut. How many more years of cutting will it take? Will people who are interested in a career in writing or producing tie into CBC, or will they go south or to Great Britain to do their life work?

March 25, 1991
Government Orders
This kind of message is sending a lot of good people away unnecessarily. If the government wants to provide some stability to CBC, it should make it quite clear that was the last cut and there will be no more.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development
subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to ask the hon. member what he thinks. If budgets have increased year after year since 1984, how can they be characterized as cuts? If he believes that CBC should be given a blank cheque over other more needy institutions or people in the country, how does he expect people who are taking cuts in social spending and all sorts of other areas across the country, at all levels of government, municipal and provincial levels, to be able to deal with the fact that CBC expects to have year after year after year excessive spending habits?
How does the hon. member expect CBC to be able to carry on with its profligate spending with a blank cheque and not be asked once in a while to use a little bit of good, common business sense?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I do not think that anyone expects the CBC to go on with profligate spending. I believe those were the words the hon. member used. However, I think the public expects their government to make it quite clear to CBC that it still has a role to play in this country. I think the public expects that mandate to be made quite clear.
When they go into a budget each year for two consecutive years and ask for massive cuts, it does not send signals that CBC is going to have a continuing mandate. It begins to look as if there is a policy of attack rather than of sustaining that organization.
As a government it is possible to lay out the guidelines and stick with it. If we are going to have CBC as we all think we should, then they say so. If the budget is going to be frozen, then they should say so. But they should not come in with new budgets every year with a big surprise that there is going to be $100 million cut in consecutive years.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to join in this debate with respect to the future of CBC.
The role of the CBC has been an integral part of
encouraging, developing and maintaining the cultural fabric of this nation for over half a century. The cuts that have been made to the CBC in the last couple of years have in fact affected that very fabric.
The cuts that this government has made to the CBC has had an impact in this country. Certainly Canadians have voiced their concerns. In many ridings right across the country including my own-in fact most of them-I am sure members have been hearing comments. I have been receiving both telephone calls and letters from constituents.
It so happens that I recently received a letter from a Moose Jaw resident, Cathy Anderson. She wrote a very eloquent, in fact very passionate letter. I think she outlined very well the feelings and the concerns of many Canadians, including certainly the people in my riding. I would like to read a few parts of this letter that Cathy Anderson has written. She talks first of all of radio:
I heard the Stamp Club, Just Mary stories, and my first symphony and opera, just to name a few. When CBC began TV programming, I was viewing. With CBC programming there was a certain quality that was ours, the players ours, the production ours, and unconsciously I was proud to be a Canadian.
She goes on to state:
I think that this is when I first began to have a feeling of being a Canadian, and that all Canadians across Canada were seeing or hearing our own.
She continues:
So for me CBC represents a reality of a united Canada, and with the CBC cuts I feel it will harm the ability of CBC to bind Canada as a nation. CBC is our mirror and our window.
CBC is crucial to the Canadian fabric, and to weaken it implies to me the Canadian voice no longer matters to my government.
Actually this was a letter sent to the Prime Minister with a copy to myself.
I think Cathy Anderson sums up very well the feelings of many Canadians right across the country of the cuts and the effect this government has had on the corporation.
March 25, 1991

One of the concerns about the cuts to the CBC is that regional differences and regional diversification are not going to be represented any more at the CBC. There was a report by the standing committee in 1988 which summarized that. It said: "If the CBC is to function as a genuinely national broadcasting service, then it must be rooted firmly in all regions of Canada. If the CBC ignores the regional nature of this country, its relevance, importance and effectiveness as a national broadcasting service will be reduced".
It is interesting that the cuts which have been effected at the CBC have resulted in those very regional cuts. Many of the programs that reflected the regional diversity and uniqueness of this nation are gone. One of the important factors, certainly for me living in Saskatchewan, which is not a overly populated province, is that it is important for the Saskatchewan message to get out. It is also interesting and important for us to know what is happening in the rest of the country.
Places in the maritimes, like Newfoundland, have lost programs unique to their area just as we in the west have lost programs that are unique to our area. The cuts at the television station in Saskatoon leave Saskatchewan with one television station to cover news broadcasting in the province, that is, the major news broadcasting.
It is hard to believe that a city of 200,000 people, the city of Saskatoon, has lost its television station for local news. That certainly affects people in the northern part of my riding who receive Saskatoon television. They have expressed concern that their local station is no longer reflecting some of the local issues which occur in Saskatoon.
The loss of shows such as the food show have also affected people in my riding. As mentioned earlier, loss of shows such as the Farm Business News which was broadcast on Newsworld, mean people in Saskatchewan are not given full information with respect to what is happening in agriculture in this country.
It is interesting that in the city of Regina there is a major broadcasting station, a beautiful building sitting in Wascana Park with beautiful facilities that is not being used. It has some of the best studios and best facilities in western Canada and it is sitting idle. It is a white elephant, and it is not that old. The purpose of that building in the mid-1980s was to provide regional pro-
Govemment Orders
gramming, and to develop and promote some of the culture in that area of the country. It is not doing it.
That is why we have people such as Cathy Anderson writing to me concerned that the CBC is not reflecting the various regions of this country.
If we do not reflect the regions of this nation, what have we got as a nation? In these days, with the concerns over the Constitution and the future of our country, there are many regions and areas that need the support of the CBC to tie the fabric of this nation together. The CBC is unable to do this more and more.
It is unable to reflect those areas so that we can feel that we are Canadian no matter what part of the country we live in. It is important that, as a country, we encourage regional development.
This is one of many directions that this government has taken which is having a direct impact on the regions of Canada. The CBC is one area. It also includes deregulation of transportation, cuts in VIA Rail, post offices, communications. The list goes on. Regions of this country are suffering. They are not being represented or promoted.
If this continues, it does not bode well for the future of our nation as a united nation. There has long been a feeling of western alienation, eastern alienation and northern alienation. Unless there is a concerted effort and a fundamental goal to promote regional development, then we are going to continue to suffer and to have an alienation feeling. The future of the nation is in danger.
As a nation that was born and built on regional development, we seem to have lost that objective. I feel it is very sad. I know that people in my riding feel it is very sad. Canadians right across this nation are lamenting that fact this very day.

If he has looked at the evidence at all, he knows that the budget will be bigger next year than it was this year. The proposal before us is that the size of the growth will be less than it has been other years, but they are not in fact cutbacks.

March 25, 1991

I am glad the member spoke because he mentioned a brand new CBC building in Regina. He called it a "white elephant" that is now sitting empty.
I asked him when the building was put up. His friend over there said it was 1985. If it was built in 1985, it was on the drawing board two and three years before that, and maybe planned four or five years before that.
If the CBC could plan a building roughly 10 years before the so-called cuts came in, is that not a symptom of a fat-cat corporation that is spending money recklessly and deserves to have its budget reined in a little bit in order to be a little bit more conscientious with a taxpayer's dollar.
If a building in Regina can sit there empty because of poor planning and too much money, is it not time that we cut back the authority of the CBC just a little bit so that its growth in spending will slow down?

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is no doubt true that the CBC facility in Regina was planned many years ago, before this government came to power, knowing that its objective would be to destroy CBC as a national network. The building is not sitting empty; the CBC still broadcasts its news programs from there. But it is largely empty. It is not being used to its full capacity. The reason that it was built was to provide a facility for regional programming, to highlight some of the cultural and regional aspects of that area of the country. Now it cannot fulfil that mandate.
The member talks about the growth of the CBC. He should go out to Saskatoon and tell the people in Saskatoon that the CBC is growing, and do it in front of the former CBC television station. He should come to Moose Jaw and tell the people that the CBC is growing. When he is there, he can remind them of the cuts of This Week right across western Canada; This Week in B.C. is gone. Sportsline, Down to Earth, Forum, Diversity, Network Night Off, parades, annual sports dinners, and Christmas concerts have all been cut from British Columbia.
In Regina we have lost the food show, which was a national show from Regina. We have lost agricultural programs. In western Canada, the CBC agriculture affairs person, George Price, retired and his position was cut. In fact, his colleagues in the agriculture standing
committee were also lamenting the fact that agriculture would no longer be getting the thorough representation that it should. He should talk to his colleagues on that side of the House on the committee and find out if it has been growing.
The member should come to Saskatchewan and tell people that the CBC is growing. It is not growing. It is not being representative. He should tell francophones in Saskatchewan that CBC is growing. The only French network programming in western Canada is on the CBC; one channel on CBC-TV and one channel on the radio, period. That is a service.
Come to Saskatchewan and tell people that the CBC is growing. It is not growing.

subtopic: ALLOTTED DAY, S. O. 81-CANADIAN BROADCASTING CORPORATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate this opportunity to address the motion presented by the hon. member for Mount Royal and to speak on a matter which is of great importance to all Canadians.
I can readily understand the member's concern for the continued strength and well-being of our national public broadcaster, the CBC. I would like to assure the hon. member that the government shares that concern and to ask her to understand that the restructuring of the CBC is not a dismantling of this great public broadcaster; rather, it is a response to changing circumstances and changing times.
There is no question that many businesses and individual Canadians are having to adjust to the present economic circumstances. This is always a difficult exercise but often the result is that one is better equipped for a changed environment. This may well be what the CBC is presently going through.
I would first like to make one thing clear. More than 1,600 CBC transmitters remain on the air serving Canadians from coast to coast. This is something that tends to be forgotten amid all the emotional pleas and cries of woe over the future of CBC. The CBC television service reaches 99 per cent of Canadians in both isolated regions and the large cities in Canada. Those 99 per cent of Canadians continue to receive CBC national and regional television. We have all been made aware that these are tough times. But they are also different times, very different from the 1950s when the CBC was the only channel in town. Different times require different thinking, different approaches, different strategies.
March 25, 1991

While I admire the hon. member's impassioned defence of the CBC and while I respect her tenacity for keeping the issue of the importance of the CBC alive before this House, I respectfully suggest that the hon. member should recognize that nothing is static and that one should adopt an outlook more relevant to today's environment and circumstances and to the rest of the 1990s.
It would be nice if we as Canadians could afford to say to the CBC: "Okay, here is an additional $100 million for this year. Yes, next year you can count on bigger increases from Parliament". But where is the money going to come from? We live in a time of severe economic restraint. Canadians everywhere are reassessing priorities. They are struggling to live within their means and they must balance their resources.
More importantly, asking the CBC to do all the things the hon. member would like to do, and asking Parliament to give it the money to do all of those things, fails to take into account the real environment in which CBC operates.
To be sure, dreams and ideals are all worth pursuing, but let us be practical. In our pursuit of a vision for the CBC, let us be a little more realistic, a little more modern. To do that, we have to place the CBC's mandate and its recent restructuring into the proper context.
The context is this. Broadcasting is a tough, competitive business that is constantly changing. Money is tight for private and for public enterprises alike and money is tight for all broadcasters, not just the CBC.
If we are going to ensure that CBC continues to provide a strong, quality Canadian television service, let us recognize the reality it finds itself in and embrace practical solutions, practical strategies so that CBC remains the cornerstone, not only of Canadian broadcasting but, indeed, of Canadian culture.
We must change our way of looking at things, of looking at the CBC, of thinking about what it should be doing. There is little to be gained by using old thinking and old solutions to address new challenges and changing circumstances that are vastly different today than even just 20 years ago.
Government Orders
What kind of environment is CBC facing? Well, as Mr. Veilleux explained in announcing the CBC's restructuring; among other things, the CBC has experienced a drop in advertising revenues. It has additional expenses as a result of inflation and of covering unforeseen world events, such as the war in the gulf.
The CBC is not alone. The entire Canadian broadcasting system is facing similar circumstances; rising costs, shrinking audiences, reduced advertising revenues and tougher competition.
Private broadcasters are also facing dramatically rising programming costs and shrinking advertising revenues. People do not watch as much television as they used to and the average television viewing in Canada is one hour less per week than it was ten years ago. Ten years ago there were a total of 103 television stations in Canada. Today, there are 129.
In 1985, CBC Television was watched by 30.6 per cent of the English-speaking Canadian audience. In 1989, this figure had dropped to 25.6 per cent.
Since 1985, the CITY network has lost 21 per cent of its audience.
The cost of programming has more than tripled in the last 10 years.
The shrinking audiences and rising costs have had a profound effect on the Canadian broadcasting system, not only on CBC, but on the private broadcasters as well.
The CBC is but one of many broadcasters that has had to change the way it operates. Other public broadcasters and private broadcasters, too, have been forced to change the way they operate to deal with these pressures. For instance, in 1987, TV Ontario and Access Alberta had to change their programming schedules substantially in response to financial pressures.
Radio Quebec has closed production centres in recent years.
The CTV network had to lay off 10 per cent of its total staff in 1987 in response to rising costs and decreasing revenues.

March 25, 1991
Supply
Private broadcasting's profits totalled 19 per cent of revenues in 1985, and then dropped to just 7.5 per cent of revenues by 1989.
This situation is not unique to Canada. In the United States, the big three networks' share of the viewing audience has plummeted from 90 per cent down to 60 per cent in just over the last 10 years.
The economics of broadcasting is changing. The structure of broadcasting is constantly evolving. This is happening in Canada and all around the world.
This is the reality of broadcasting today. This is the situation that the CBC and other broadcasters must adapt to.
Broadcasters in general, but public broadcasters especially, must adopt new strategies to deal with the ever changing broadcasting environment. This is the situation that Parliament has already faced up to and accepted. That is why Parliament passed a new Broadcasting Act recently. TTtis followed months of consultation, debate, committee hearings, discussions in the media, not to mention a number of studies.
The new act updates the CBC's mandate in a very practical manner that ensures that CBC will be a relevant national and regional public broadcaster, not only for the 1990s, but well beyond.
This mandate reflects the fact that the CBC is not the only broadcaster in Canada today. It is one of many services, each vying for the attention of the Canadian viewing public.
There is a huge, diverse Canadian broadcasting system out there with private, provincial and local cable programming services. The CBC's mandate reflects this reality. The CBC's restructuring reflects all of this.
Indeed, it has been suggested in numerous studies over the last few years that the CBC should be restructured. For example, the Federal Cultural Policy Review Committee proposed quite emphatically that the CBC withdraw from local programming and concentrate its efforts on regional production.
More recently, the Caplan-Sauvageau task force said of CBC's regional mandate, and I quote:
The time has come for the CBC to send out a psychological message: That it is prepared to re-examine its commitments to a certain level of facilities and even to certain kinds of programming for the sake of a few hours of something more distinctive with higher production values and lower cost per viewer.
